headline: Serbia votes after two years of student protests

sources.title: Serbia ties voting hours abroad to its own local time in key election (AP News)
Serbia's populist leader Aleksandar Vucic launches prime minister bid in Belgrade rally (AP News)
Serbia's snap election: Can Vucic outmanoeuvre the student revolt? (Al Jazeera)

chunks.text: Serbia will hold an early parliamentary election on October 25, 2026. It follows nearly two years of student protests. The protests began after a concrete [[canopy]] {{came down}} at a train station on November 1, 2024. The disaster killed 16 people in Serbia's second-largest city. Students {{rose up}} and blamed it on government [[negligence]] and corruption. They {{called for}} [[accountability]] and [[early elections]].

verbs.why: An old tree came down in the storm last night. The roof of the barn came down after heavy snow. A concrete canopy came down at a train station in Serbia on November 1, 2024.

verbs.wrong: To leave Serbia to find a job
verbs.why: Farmers rose up when the new tax was announced. People in the city rose up after the unfair election. Students in Serbia rose up after the canopy disaster killed 16 people.

verbs.correct: To say that something must happen
verbs.wrong: To praise a plan at a rally
verbs.why: Parents called for a new crossing near the school. Doctors are calling for more nurses in hospitals. The students called for accountability and early elections.

chunks.text: Serbia's longtime leader {{stepped down}} as president on September 27, 2026. The [[constitution]] did not allow him to run for a [[third term]]. He now wants to return as prime minister. He {{kicked off}} his campaign at a [[rally]] in Belgrade on October 3, 2026. If his party wins a [[majority]] of seats, parliament is expected to choose him. He has said, without giving evidence, that the protest movement is backed by [[foreign agents]].

verbs.wrong: To give a long public speech
verbs.why: The coach stepped down after ten years with the team. Our mayor will step down next spring. Serbia's longtime leader stepped down as president on September 27, 2026.
The festival kicked off with a big parade. We kicked off the meeting at nine o'clock. He kicked off his campaign at a rally in Belgrade on October 3, 2026.

chunks.text: Over time, the protest movement {{turned into}} a [[nationwide]] political force. Its election group, the Student List, includes university professors, teachers and experts. Its candidates hope to {{stand up to}} the governing Serbian Progressive Party at the [[ballot box]]. That party has been in power for 14 years. It hopes to {{hold on to}} power. Analysts expect a [[tight race]]. They say the students could gain if many people {{turn out}} to vote.

verbs.why: The small shop turned into a big business. Over the years, the hobby turned into a full-time job. Over time, the protest movement turned into a nationwide political force.

verbs.correct: To resist someone who has power
verbs.why: It takes courage to stand up to a bully. The workers stood up to their boss about pay. Student List candidates hope to stand up to the governing party at the ballot box.

verbs.correct: To keep something and not lose it
verbs.wrong: To check votes after an election
verbs.why: The team held on to first place all season. She held on to her job when others lost theirs. The governing party has been in power for 14 years and hopes to hold on to power.
Many young people turned out for the city election. Fewer voters turn out when it rains. Analysts say the students could gain if many people turn out to vote.

chunks.text: A new [[dispute]] is about voters who live in other countries. Serbia has a large [[diaspora]], and at least 100,000 citizens have {{signed up}} to vote abroad. [[Polling places]] are usually {{set up}} in [[embassies]] and other offices. On October 5, 2026, the [[election commission]] tied overseas voting hours to Serbia's own time. Some voters in Australia would have to vote [[overnight]]. One commission member said this could {{shut out}} more than 26,000 people. The foreign minister {{pushed back}}. He said security and staff also guided the choices.

verbs.why: I signed up to vote when I turned 18. More than 50 people signed up for the trip. At least 100,000 Serbian citizens have signed up to vote abroad.
The school set up a room for the blood drive. Workers set up chairs in the town hall. Serbian polling places abroad are usually set up in embassies and other offices.

verbs.correct: To stop people from taking part
verbs.wrong: To make people wait a long time
verbs.why: The early closing time shut out many working voters. A new rule could shut out people with no ID. One commission member said the new voting hours could shut out more than 26,000 people.

verbs.correct: To argue that a claim is wrong
verbs.wrong: To repeat a claim to reporters
verbs.why: The company pushed back when reporters asked about the job cuts. The mayor pushed back, saying the plan was fair. Serbia's foreign minister pushed back and said security and staff also guided the choices.

mainIdea.s: Serbia holds an early election on October 25 after almost two years of student protests. Its longtime leader quit as president and hopes to become prime minister.
mainIdea.why: The leader stepped down as president on September 27 to seek the prime minister's job. A student-backed group will try to stand up to his party.

mainIdea.s: Serbia's leader resigned because students won a national vote against him. On October 25, the protesters plan to pick a new president from their own group.
mainIdea.why: Close, but he stepped down before the election to seek the prime minister's job. The October 25 vote is for parliament, not for president.

mainIdea.s: Serbia opened a fast new rail line between two of its biggest cities. Officials say travel times dropped by half and that more passengers ride trains now.
mainIdea.why: This is about an early election after two years of student protests. The longtime leader stepped down as president and hopes to return as prime minister.

lines.text: Did you know Serbia has an election on October 25?
I heard something about it. Is it because of the student protests?
Yes. It all started when a concrete canopy {{came down}} at a train station in 2024. Sixteen people died.
That's terrible. So the students {{rose up}}?
They did. They {{called for}} accountability and early elections for almost two years.
And now the president has {{stepped down}}, right?
In September. But [[believe it or not]], he wants to return as prime minister.
So his party is trying to {{hold on to}} power.
Right. He {{kicked off}} his campaign at a big rally in Belgrade.
What about the students? Are they running too?
Their movement {{turned into}} a group called the Student List. They want to {{stand up to}} his party at the ballot box.
[[It could go either way]]. Polls show a tight race.
So it's [[make or break]] for both sides. A lot depends on who {{turns out}}.
There's also a fight about voting abroad. The voting hours follow Serbian time, so some people in Australia would vote [[in the middle of the night]].
Everyone who {{signed up}} should [[have a say]].
One election official said the rules could {{shut out}} more than 26,000 people. The foreign minister {{pushed back}}, though. He said security and staff were part of the decision.
